fields.Front: Walk through how you'd build one RL task end to end, from “models are bad at X” to a task ready to ship.
fields.Back:
• A task = instruction + environment + verifier; reward = the verifier's score. Purpose: measure progress or make progress.
  • Find a failure mode rather than inventing a task; judge value by economic value (what do people get paid for?).
  • Check it's fair, then classify why the model failed.
  • Build a reproducible environment: realistic, coding-first, no leaks.
  • Write a verifier that checks outcomes; oracle solution → 1.0, doing nothing → 0.0.
  • Hunt for reward hacks by sampling.
  • Calibrate with pass rates across models.
  • QC: static checks → LM rubrics → automated trials → judge reviews the trials → expert review.

source_label: RL Environments › 1. What is a Task?

fields.Front: What are the four sources of failure modes? For each, what do you get for free, and what's the hard part?
fields.Back:
• Real usage by experts: you get the instruction, expected result and how it fails. Hard part: reproducing the messy real-world environment.
  • Raw domain data: learn the domain and who uses the data, find data that changes over time; give the state at t−1, ask for t. GitHub is the best example (commits, issues, PRs).
  • App-company traces: richest signal (user retries, complaints). Only counts if the failure comes from the model, not the app. Open question: does selling them give away your moat?
  • Brute force / synthetic: optimization tasks where people push a number. Needs an easy 0 (baseline) and 1 (target), scores measurable across variants, easy-to-change inputs; ideally the solution can be found by search.

fields.Front: A model fails your task. How do you decide whether this failure is worth turning into a task?
fields.Back:
• Fairness test: an expert given the task shouldn't fail the same way the model does.
  • Sources of unfairness: instruction underspecified, vague or contradictory · environment lacks information or infra fails (can a solution even be found?) · success doesn't reflect reality (inflated expectations) · success depends on implementation, not result.
  • If fair, classify the failure: lack of knowledge / real-world experience · solved it but broke something else · lazy, stopped early and claimed done · cheated (reward hacking).

source_label: RL Environments › 2. Selecting Good Failure Modes

fields.Front: What are all the ways a task can give away its answer or reveal that it's a test, and how do you prevent each?
fields.Back:
• Leakage: git history, metadata left in the environment, dependencies used during setup.
  • Contamination: a public solution (e.g. a merged PR) may be in pre-training. Look for answers that seem recalled from memory.
  • Eval-awareness phrases: “the verifier will check…”, “you have n seconds”.
  • Instructions: state the goal, not the implementation; don't over-describe the environment; no READMEs or files acting as a second instruction; let the agent discover things.
  • Internet access: on = security and reproducibility risks; off = consistency, but less realism and more eval awareness. Isolation is the sandbox provider's job.

source_label: RL Environments › 3.2. Leakage and Eval Awareness

fields.Front: How do you design a verifier, and when does it need an LM judge instead of deterministic checks?
fields.Back:
• Three rules: check only what the instruction asks for · check results, implementation is a black box · no artificial difficulty (e.g. narrowing a target number).
  • Choices: binary or continuous, partial credit, baseline, negative scores (24/25 tests? 10ms target? taxes half filed?).
  • Deterministic vs judge: show a candidate answer to 10 experts. All agree → deterministic (tests, performance, values in mocks, exact strings, float tolerance). Could disagree → judge/rubric (diagnosis, legal, accounting).
  • For judges: align with experts · self-consistency / majority voting · a few contrasting examples in the prompt.
  • Sanity checks: oracle → 1.0 every time, doing nothing → 0.0; same result across runs (GPU hardware variance).

fields.Front: Why does reward hacking matter, how do you harden a task against it, and how do you actively find hacks?
fields.Back:
• Why: rewarded cheating gets reinforced → misalignment risk. Defending is mostly reactive.
  • Guards: don't expose tests · protect them from tampering · checksums (SHAs) of files that must not change · separate verifier container · clean copies of files in the verifier, never the environment's.
  • Find hacks by sampling: cheat trials (give models the verifier, ask for 1.0 without solving; terminal-bench /cheat) · LM judge reads existing trials for hacks · add deterministic checks and repeat until nothing gets through.
  • Open problem: patches for specific hacks won't stop future models from finding new ones.

fields.Front: How do you calibrate a task's difficulty, and what signals tell you the task design is broken?
fields.Back:
• Calibration = pass rates (e.g. 3 of 8 samples succeed). Ideally from the task's natural difficulty, not tweaking.
  • Making an easy task harder is fine if it stays realistic: no padding with repeated work. Task stacking: ask only for y so the agent must work out and do x; not “do x, then y”.
  • Warning signs: a small hint makes pass rates jump across many models · many hints and pass rates don't move · every model fails the same way.
  • Good sign: the task tells models apart; different models struggle with different things.

fields.Front: How do you go from one good task to many without losing quality?
fields.Back:
• Scaling depends on: how parametrizable the task is (swap (tax document, filed total) pairs into environment and verifier) and how easily realistic data can be synthesized (augmentation, not ideal).
  • ~80% is QC: static checks → LM rubrics → automated trials → judge reviews the trials → expert review (quality, fairness, realism).
  • Read the trial logs.
  • Post-train on your tasks if you have the compute: learn which data drove the gains and how much it improves the model.
